top_learned_concepts: Virtualization and hypervisors as core systems concepts, including how hardware, OSes, and resource management relate
Docker/containers as application packaging and runtime environments
CI and unit testing as parts of modern development workflow
Operating systems and cross-system/platform context, including Windows and interest in Linux
top_struggle_clusters: Distinguishing related infrastructure concepts: Docker vs VMs, virtualization vs Hyper-V specifics, and how virtual networking/checkpoints work
Applying testing in practice: what unit tests to write, how testing differs across languages, and how to test bots/APIs/databases/web applications
Understanding collaboration/CI at scale: GitHub pushing workflows, multiple developers, merge conflicts, branch protections, and what CI does or does not catch
Connecting tools to purpose and scope: how important Docker is, what happens without a hypervisor, and fitting these topics into the bigger picture
future_interest_clusters: More hands-on depth with Docker, virtualization, and Linux/alternative OS environments
Broader and deeper testing coverage, especially for APIs, databases, and possibly SQL
CI/CD beyond testing, especially deployment workflows to cloud platforms like Azure or AWS
Team-based development practices for larger GitHub projects and collaborative workflows
mismatches: Students reported learning key terms and concepts in systems/virtualization, but many questions show uncertainty about conceptual boundaries between containers, VMs, hypervisors, and platform-specific tools
Unit testing appeared in both learned and struggled responses, suggesting students feel introduced to it but not yet confident applying it to authentic project contexts
CI was perceived as learned, but reflections indicate unresolved understanding of how CI interacts with collaboration practices such as reviews, branch protection, and integration failures
Difficulty ratings were moderately high overall, consistent with reflections describing these topics as broad and hard to fit into a coherent big picture
teaching_adjustments: Teach a comparison frame explicitly: container vs VM vs hypervisor vs operating system, with one visual diagram and one concrete scenario for each
Add a short application-focused testing mini-workshop where students generate test cases for a web app, API endpoint, or bot, emphasizing how to decide what to test
Clarify the boundary between unit, integration, and end-to-end tests so students can map testing methods to different project components
Demonstrate a realistic GitHub workflow with branches, pull requests, required checks, and an example of code that passes alone but fails after integration
Include a brief 'why this matters' segment for Docker and virtualization to address questions about importance, tradeoffs, and industry use
Provide one cross-language testing bridge example, since students are asking how testing ideas transfer between C#, Python, SQL, and API contexts
followup_exit_ticket_questions: What is still unclear about the difference between containers, virtual machines, and hypervisors?
If you had to add tests to one part of your current project, what part would you choose and what would you test first?
What aspect of GitHub/CI collaboration feels most confusing right now: branching, pull requests, merge conflicts, required checks, or deployment?
Would a hands-on Linux/Docker lab help you connect the big picture? Why or why not?
What kind of real-project testing example would be most useful next: API, database, Discord bot, or web app?
ai_summary.short_instructor_summary: Students perceived meaningful learning in virtualization, hypervisors, Docker, CI, and unit testing, but their questions show that understanding is still mostly introductory. The strongest struggle pattern is not lack of exposure but difficulty distinguishing related concepts and applying them in real project settings. Testing is a key example: students say they learned unit testing, yet they still want guidance on what to test, how testing transfers across languages/tools, and how to test more complex systems. A second major need is workflow coherence: students want the big picture of how Docker, GitHub, CI, and multi-developer collaboration fit together in authentic software practice. The most actionable next step is to move from topic introduction to structured comparisons and integrated demonstrations.

study_guide.title: CSCI 2910 Study Guide – Week of 2026-04-19
study_guide.overview: This week introduced several connected ideas: virtualization and hypervisors, Docker/containers, operating systems, CI, and unit testing. Many students recognized the main terms, but the biggest challenge was seeing how the pieces fit together in real projects. Use this guide to review the vocabulary, clarify key comparisons, and practice applying the ideas to software development workflows.
key_takeaways_to_review: Virtualization and hypervisors: review how hardware, operating systems, and virtualized resources relate.
Docker/containers: remember that containers package what an application needs to run.
Operating systems context: connect course topics to Windows, Linux, and cross-platform development environments.
CI and testing: review how automated tests fit into a development workflow.
Unit testing: focus not just on writing tests, but on deciding what parts of a program should be tested first.
Big picture: these topics are related through deployment, reproducibility, collaboration, and reliable software delivery.
common_sticking_points: Telling apart containers, virtual machines, hypervisors, and operating systems.
Understanding platform-specific ideas such as Hyper-V, virtual switches/networking, and checkpoints.
Knowing what makes Docker important or when it is worth using.
Choosing useful unit tests for web apps, APIs, bots, and other server-side projects.
Understanding how testing ideas transfer across languages and tools like C#, Python, APIs, and databases/SQL contexts without assuming the exact syntax is the same everywhere.
practice_prompts: Explain, in your own words, the difference between a container, a VM, a hypervisor, and an operating system.
Write a 3–4 sentence answer to: Why might a developer use Docker in a project?
Choose one project component you know well and list 3 things that could be unit tested.
Describe what CI does after code is pushed to a repository.
Think through this question: if two developers each make changes that work separately, what additional workflow steps besides tests might help protect the main branch?
Write down one thing that belongs to the 'big picture' of modern development: environment setup, testing, collaboration, packaging, or deployment—and explain how it connects to the others.
example_problems: Comparison practice: Fill in a chart with four rows—OS, hypervisor, VM, container—and write one short purpose statement for each.
Testing practice: For a server-side function that validates user input, list 3 test cases: one normal case, one edge case, and one invalid case.
API thinking practice: If an endpoint is supposed to return data for a valid request and an error for a bad request, what two basic tests would you want?
Collaboration practice: Imagine a GitHub workflow with branches, pull requests, and required checks. What problem does each step help reduce?
practical_examples: A container example: packaging an app with its runtime/dependencies so it runs more consistently across machines.
A virtualization example: running another operating system environment on the same hardware through a hypervisor.
A unit testing example: checking whether a helper function returns the expected result for known inputs.
A CI example: automatically running tests when code is pushed to GitHub so issues are caught early.
self_check_questions: Can I clearly distinguish Docker from a VM without using the terms as if they mean the same thing?
Can I describe what a hypervisor does at a high level?
Do I understand that learning unit testing includes both how to write tests and how to choose what to test?
Can I explain one way CI helps a team, and one thing CI alone does not solve?
Can I name one part of the overall workflow that still feels unclear so I can ask about it next class?
before_next_class: Review your notes on virtualization, hypervisors, containers, and CI as one connected topic rather than isolated terms.
Make a one-page comparison sheet: container vs VM vs hypervisor vs OS.
Pick one current or past coding project and identify 2–3 unit tests you would add first.
If you use GitHub, trace the path from 'write code' to 'push' to 'checks run' to 'merge' and note where confusion starts.
Come to class with one specific question about either testing in real projects, Docker/Linux environments, or team collaboration workflows.
